# Sample Size for Correlation Studies {#sec-correlation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Distinguish estimating correlation from testing a correlation.
- Identify independence and model assumptions.
:::

## The idea

A correlation study may aim to estimate a population correlation with acceptable precision, test the correlation against a prespecified null value, or compare independent correlations. For the Pearson correlation, a common approximate approach uses Fisher’s transformation $z=\operatorname{atanh}(r)$ with variance approximately $1/(n-3)$. Precision on the transformed scale is not identical to a symmetric half-width on the original correlation scale.

## When and how to apply it

Pearson correlation describes linear association and can be affected by outliers, restricted ranges and nonlinearity. The present calculator uses a documented uncorrected Fisher-z normal approximation; it is not an exact Pearson t-test power calculation.

## Formula at a glance

$$
z_r=\operatorname{atanh}(r)=\frac12\ln\left(\frac{1+r}{1-r}\right)
$$


## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
A study anticipates $r=0.30$ between BMI and systolic blood pressure. Compare the research questions “estimate $r$ precisely” and “test $r$ against zero.”
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Do not interpret correlation as causation or use the independent-correlation method for repeated measures from the same participants.
:::

## Hands-on exercise

Plan a correlation study with an anticipated $r=0.30$ and examine the sample size for different precision or power targets.

Correlation precision and correlation testing are different design objectives.
